The parasitic jaeger (Stercorarius parasiticus) is an Arctic-breeding seabird that exhibits remarkable life-history traits shaped by its kleptoparasitic foraging strategy. Field studies from the Canadian tundra indicate that newly hatched chicks emerge at a modest body mass of approximately 33.65 grams [Wwb = approximately 33.65 grams], reflecting the substantial yolk investment required to sustain embryonic development. The initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg is considerably higher, recorded at 50.3 grams [Ww0 = 50.3 grams], a value that situates the parasitic jaeger among the larger-bodied Arctic skuas and reflects the large yolk reserve needed to support embryonic development during the short Arctic breeding season. Hatching occurs after a relatively brief incubation period of approximately 26.25 days [ab = approximately 26.25 days], a duration consistently observed when eggs are maintained at the optimal artificial incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This ontogenetic timing, while efficient for a species breeding in a short Arctic summer, is followed by a prolonged postnatal development phase before independence is achieved. The nesting pair jointly attends the nest, and the single brood of one to two chicks demands intensive provisioning throughout the nestling period, underscoring the energetic challenge of raising offspring in a resource-limited environment.

Sexual maturation in this species proceeds gradually, with young birds attaining puberty at approximately 82.5 days after hatching [tp = approximately 82.5 days after hatching] when reared under the thermoneutral conditions typical of their active metabolic range (40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]). This developmental milestone, representing the onset of gonadal activity, is reached several weeks prior to the attainment of full adult body mass. Females ultimately achieve a substantially larger size than males, with the ultimate wet weight for adult females recorded at 478 grams [Wwi = 478 grams], whereas adult males capsize at a more modest 413 grams [Wwi = 413 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism, consistent with patterns observed in congeneric species, likely reflects divergent selective pressures: larger body size in females may enhance fecundity and egg production capacity, while the slightly smaller male body mass may confer greater maneuverability during aerial pursuit of avian hosts. The growth trajectory from hatchling to adult is rapid, driven by the high-protein diet of fish, lemmings, and bird eggs that the parents deliver to the nest.

Chicks achieve sustained flight — the fledging milestone — after approximately 27.5 days [tx = approximately 27.5 days] from hatching when reared at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], a period typical of Arctic-nesting charadriiforms. This relatively short fledging period is critical for escaping terrestrial predators and for migrating south before the onset of winter. Post-fledging, juveniles remain partially dependent on parental provisioning for several additional weeks while honing their flight muscles and foraging skills. The transition to nutritional independence is gradual, and young birds are often observed accompanying adults on foraging trips well into the late summer. This extended period of post-fledging care likely enhances juvenile survival during the critical first year of life, a time when inexperienced individuals face elevated mortality risks from starvation and predation.

Reproductive activity commences relatively early compared to many other seabirds of similar body size. The time since birth at first brood is estimated at approximately 1204.5 days [tR = approximately 1204.5 days] when birds are maintained under the thermal conditions of their active metabolic period (40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]), a delay that reflects the time required for somatic growth and territory acquisition before initiating reproduction. This translates to an onset of first reproduction at roughly three to four years of age, a pattern consistent with the species' moderately paced life history. Females typically produce a single clutch annually, laying between one and two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between one and two eggs per clutch], and most pairs attempt approximately one to two breeding events per year [F_R_i = approximately one to two breeding events per year]. This low annual reproductive output is compensated by relatively high adult survival rates, typical of long-lived seabirds that invest heavily in each offspring. The Arctic breeding season imposes a narrow temporal window for successful reproduction, and any delay in nesting can severely compromise chick survival.

Longevity records for the parasitic jaeger indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 31.1 years [am = approximately 31.1 years] under the thermoneutral conditions reflective of its active metabolic range (40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]), a duration comparable to that of other Stercorariidae and underscoring the species' reliance on high adult survivorship. Mark-recapture studies from the Canadian Arctic and Fennoscandian populations confirm that individuals can persist for over three decades, with the oldest documented wild bird exceeding this estimate. Such longevity allows experienced breeders to accumulate substantial reproductive success over their lifetimes through iterative nesting attempts, despite the constraints imposed by the short Arctic summer and the energetic demands of kleptoparasitic foraging. Field observations indicate that adult mortality in this species is primarily driven by stochastic events such as severe storms and prey scarcity during the non-breeding season, rather than by senescence alone.
